newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwanese praise Deng, but uncertain about ties.
newsitem.headline: Taiwanese praise Deng, but uncertain about ties.

text.p: Most Taiwanese believe China's late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping made a valuable contribution to the huge nation but said on Friday they were uncertain about future relations between the two political rivals.

Some 55 percent of 888 people interviewed by the United Daily News said they were positive about Deng's contribution to Chinese history, compared with nine percent who said the patriarch made no contribution.

Deng, the man whose pragmatic policies transformed a backward Stalinist state into an economic powerhouse, died late on Wednesday of complications from Parkinson's disease and a lung infection in Beijing.
Another newspaper poll conducted by the China Times showed that 42 percent of 972 respondents said Deng's contribution was greater than that of China's late Chairman Mao Zedong. Mao died in 1976.
Less than seven percent said Mao's contribution was greater than Deng's.
Sixty percent of respondents in the China Times poll said Deng's death had "no impact whatsoever" on Taiwan, echoing Thursday's appeals for calm by senior government officials.
Many people said they were uncertain about future relations between the Nationalist Taiwan and Communist China as well as the political situation in the post-Deng era.
More than a third of people were unclear about the direction of Taiwan-China ties, while 26 percent believed the mainland would be in turmoil with Deng's passing, the polls said.
But some people were undaunted.
"Deng Xiaoping? If he dies, he dies. There is nothing to be afraid of," 34-year-old school teacher Tsui Teh-hsing said in a Taipei park.
More than half of Taiwan's people believed China would carry on economic reforms initiated by Deng and China would become more democratic, the United Daily News said.
The island's usually super-sensitive stock market has shrugged off political fears, rising 0.28 percent on Thursday and 1.47 percent on Friday.
The Taiwan dollar also rebounded to T$27.567 against to the U.S. dollar at midday on Friday, compared with Thursday's T$27.625 close.
Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui appeared to be calm, saying his island should not overreact to Deng's death. He said Taiwan had weathered worse storms during a recent missile crisis.
Lee was referring to missile tests China conducted off Taiwan in March last year, designed to intimidate Taipei ahead of its presidential election that month.
"It (Deng's death) had happened and the stock market rose... We should set our heart at ease," Lee was quoted as telling a group of national assemblymen.
"Why should you worry if I am not worried?" Lee said.
But on Thursday the island, which Beijing has regarded as a renegade province since a civil war ended in 1949, maintained a military alert and advised its people to stay calm.

When asked how he felt about Deng's death, taxi driver Huang Wen-Cheng said: "I hope the mainland will not take any military action (against Taiwan) so that Taiwan can still maintain its peace and prosperity."
Beijing refuses to rule out the use of force to retake Taiwan. The island says it wants reunification, but insists the island keep its democracatic and free market systems.
